Hobbits — Periannath

Les Hobbits, appelés Periannath en sindarin et souvent Halfelins par les Hommes, sont un petit peuple apparenté aux Humains. Ils sont suffisamment distincts par leur taille, leur longévité, leur constitution et leur histoire pour être traités comme une Race propre. Ils restent longtemps peu connus des grands peuples de la Terre du Milieu, car leurs communautés sont petites, rurales et éloignées des principales guerres.

Leurs premiers foyers connus se trouvent à l’est des Monts Brumeux, dans la vallée de l’Anduin. Au cours du Troisième Âge, plusieurs groupes migrèrent vers l’ouest et s’établirent progressivement en Eriador. Les trois grandes traditions hobbits sont les Pieds-velus, les Forts et les Pâles. Elles doivent être traitées comme des Cultures et non comme des Races séparées.

Migrations et installation en Eriador

Les migrations hobbits furent progressives et s’étendirent sur plusieurs générations. Elles furent généralement motivées par la recherche de terres sûres, fertiles et adaptées à leur mode de vie plutôt que par la conquête.

Après plusieurs étapes en Eriador, une grande partie des Hobbits s’établit dans la région qui devint la Comté. Celle-ci fut accordée à leurs ancêtres par l’autorité du Royaume du Nord. Après la disparition des institutions d’Arnor, les Hobbits continuèrent à vivre selon leurs propres coutumes avec très peu d’intervention extérieure.

Apparence

Les Hobbits sont beaucoup plus petits que les Hommes et généralement plus petits que les Khazâd. Leur taille moyenne se situe autour d’un mètre, avec des variations selon les lignées. Leur corps est compact et robuste plutôt que fragile.

Leurs pieds sont larges, solides et couverts d’un poil épais. La plante est suffisamment résistante pour qu’ils marchent habituellement pieds nus. Les chaussures sont donc rares et réservées à des conditions particulières.

Longévité et maturité

Les Hobbits vivent plus longtemps que les Hommes ordinaires. Beaucoup atteignent quatre-vingts ou quatre-vingt-dix ans, et certains dépassent cent ans. Dans la Comté, trente-trois ans correspond traditionnellement à la majorité.

Ils vieillissent lentement et peuvent rester actifs pendant une grande partie de leur vie. Les Hobbits âgés jouent souvent un rôle important dans la mémoire familiale et locale, notamment pour les généalogies, les propriétés et les anciennes histoires.

Santé et endurance

Les Hobbits sont généralement en bonne santé mais ne possèdent pas de résistance surnaturelle aux maladies. Leur mode de vie rural, une alimentation régulière et leur constitution robuste leur donnent une bonne résistance aux efforts ordinaires.

Ils supportent mieux les longues marches qu’on pourrait l’imaginer au regard de leur taille. Leur endurance repose davantage sur la constance que sur la vitesse ou la force brute.

Sens et discrétion

Les sens des Hobbits sont proches de ceux des Hommes et ils ne possèdent pas de vision nocturne particulière. Ils ont cependant une bonne perception de leur environnement proche et remarquent facilement les changements dans un lieu familier.

Leur capacité à se déplacer silencieusement est l’un de leurs traits les plus caractéristiques. Leur petite taille, leur démarche pieds nus et leur habitude d’éviter les surfaces bruyantes leur permettent d’approcher sans être entendus. Cette aptitude raciale doit compléter, et non remplacer, les compétences de Dissimulation et de Déplacement furtif.

Résistance morale

Les Hobbits sont moins attirés que beaucoup d’autres peuples par le pouvoir, la domination et la gloire. Ils désirent généralement un foyer sûr, une vie stable, de bonnes récoltes, de la nourriture et la compagnie de leurs proches. Cette faible ambition les rend relativement difficiles à corrompre par les promesses de puissance.

Ils ne sont pas immunisés contre l’Ombre. La peur, la jalousie, la possession ou le désir de protéger les leurs peuvent toujours être exploités. Leur résistance vient surtout du fait que les formes les plus classiques de tentation ont peu d’intérêt pour eux.

Tempérament

Les Hobbits sont généralement prudents, sociables et attachés aux habitudes. Ils s’intéressent beaucoup aux affaires de leur famille et de leur voisinage, tout en se montrant souvent méfiants envers les événements lointains, les étrangers et les changements brusques.

Ils valorisent le bon sens et les solutions concrètes. Les grands discours, les titres et les projets très ambitieux les impressionnent peu lorsqu’ils ne produisent aucun résultat pratique.

Famille et société

La famille est au centre de la société hobbit. Les liens de parenté sont connus avec précision et les familles étendues entretiennent des relations régulières par les mariages, les visites, les héritages et les fêtes. Le nom de famille possède une forte importance sociale.

Le mariage est généralement monogame. Les enfants grandissent dans un environnement communautaire où parents, oncles, tantes, cousins et voisins participent à leur éducation. Les différences de richesse existent, mais elles ne produisent pas une noblesse guerrière comparable à celle de nombreux royaumes humains.

Autorité, coutumes et propriété

Les institutions hobbits sont simples et les autorités disposent généralement de pouvoirs limités. Les coutumes locales, la réputation et la pression sociale règlent une grande partie des conflits. Les questions de propriété, de limites de terrain, d’héritage et de succession sont néanmoins prises très au sérieux.

Les objets transmis dans une famille possèdent souvent une valeur importante en raison de leur histoire. Les cadeaux, les anniversaires et les échanges entre familles jouent un rôle notable dans la vie sociale.

Habitat et confort

Les Hobbits sont célèbres pour les demeures creusées dans les collines, souvent appelées trous de Hobbit ou smials. Les plus grandes peuvent comprendre de nombreuses chambres, cuisines, salons, caves, garde-manger et couloirs. D’autres Hobbits vivent dans des maisons construites en surface lorsque le terrain s’y prête mieux.

Ils accordent une grande valeur au confort, à la propreté, à la chaleur et aux réserves de nourriture. Leur conception de la prospérité repose davantage sur un foyer bien entretenu et une terre fertile que sur les monuments ou les trésors.

Agriculture, jardinage et alimentation

L’agriculture constitue la base de nombreuses communautés hobbits. Ils cultivent céréales, légumes, fruits, herbes, houblon et diverses plantes utiles. Le jardinage est très répandu et certains Hobbits possèdent une excellente connaissance pratique de la flore locale.

La nourriture occupe une place importante dans leur vie quotidienne. Ils apprécient plusieurs repas, les recettes familiales, les repas collectifs et les auberges. La bière et, aux périodes tardives, l’herbe à pipe font partie des traditions les plus connues de la Comté.

Artisanat et commerce

Les Hobbits sont de bons artisans dans les domaines utiles à la vie quotidienne : menuiserie, couture, cuisine, poterie, agriculture et fabrication de petits outils. Ils produisent rarement des ouvrages militaires, des armures lourdes ou de grandes constructions de pierre.

Le commerce existe surtout à l’échelle régionale. Les communautés peuvent importer métal, outils et tissus et exporter nourriture, bière, produits agricoles et artisanat. Peu de Hobbits deviennent marchands à longue distance.

Armes et guerre

La plupart des Hobbits ne reçoivent pas de formation militaire poussée. Les couteaux, bâtons, frondes, arcs courts et outils agricoles sont les armes les plus naturelles. Les armes conçues pour les Hommes sont souvent trop grandes pour eux.

Ils sont particulièrement adroits lorsqu’ils lancent des pierres ou utilisent une fronde. Leur coordination et leur pratique depuis l’enfance leur donnent une précision surprenante. Les armures sont rares ; lorsqu’une communauté doit se défendre, elle privilégie la connaissance du terrain, les haies, les chemins, les tirs à distance et les embuscades.

Magie et religion

Les Hobbits possèdent peu de traditions magiques organisées. La magie est généralement associée aux Elfes, aux Magiciens ou aux récits anciens. Un Hobbit peut néanmoins apprendre la magie s’il reçoit une formation appropriée ; les professions magiques doivent simplement rester rares dans les Cultures traditionnelles.

Leur religion est peu institutionnalisée. Ils n’ont pas de grands temples ni de clergé visible. Leur vie spirituelle est surtout liée aux coutumes, à la famille, aux saisons, à la terre et au souvenir des morts.

Relations avec les autres peuples

Les relations avec les Hommes sont généralement pacifiques, même si les Grandes Gens sous-estiment souvent les Hobbits. Les Dúnedain du Nord protègent secrètement la Comté au Troisième Âge, sans que la majorité de ses habitants en mesure l’importance.

Les Elfes sont longtemps des figures presque légendaires pour les Hobbits. Les contacts avec les Khazâd sont plus concrets grâce aux routes et au commerce. Les Orcs et les autres serviteurs de l’Ombre sont des ennemis dangereux que les Hobbits préfèrent éviter ou combattre à distance.

Les trois grandes Cultures

Les Pieds-velus sont les plus nombreux et sont étroitement associés aux collines, aux terres agricoles et aux demeures creusées. Les Forts sont généralement plus trapus et davantage liés aux rivières, à la pêche et aux terrains humides. Les Pâles sont souvent plus grands, plus clairs de cheveux et historiquement plus proches des Elfes et des régions boisées.

Ces groupes se mélangèrent progressivement après leur migration vers l’Eriador. À une époque tardive, un Hobbit peut avoir des ancêtres issus des trois traditions ; la Culture représente alors surtout l’éducation et l’héritage familial dominant.

La Race Hobbits — Periannath doit représenter les caractéristiques communes : petite taille, longévité supérieure à celle des Hommes ordinaires, pieds résistants, déplacement naturellement silencieux, bonne coordination et résistance relative aux tentations fondées sur l’ambition.

Les restrictions professionnelles doivent être définies principalement par la Culture. Les Combattants existent mais restent peu courants, et les utilisateurs de magie sont rares. Après avoir choisi la Race, le joueur sélectionne la Culture Pieds-velus, Forts ou Pâles selon l’époque et l’origine du personnage.

Hobbits — Kuduk

Hobbits, called Periannath in Sindarin and often Halflings by Men, are a small people related to Humans. They are sufficiently distinct in size, longevity, constitution and history to be treated as a Race of their own. For a long time they remain little known to the great peoples of Middle-earth, because their communities are small, rural and far removed from the principal wars.

Their earliest known homes lie east of the Misty Mountains, in the vale of the Anduin. During the Third Age, several groups migrated westward and gradually settled in Eriador. The three great Hobbit traditions are the Harfoots, Stoors and Fallohides. They should be treated as Cultures rather than as separate Races.

Migrations and settlement in Eriador

Hobbit migrations were gradual and extended over several generations. They were usually driven by the search for safe, fertile lands suited to their way of life rather than by conquest.

After several stages of settlement in Eriador, a large part of the Hobbit population established itself in the region that became the Shire. This land was granted to their ancestors by the authority of the Northern Kingdom. After the disappearance of Arnor's institutions, the Hobbits continued to live according to their own customs with very little outside interference.

Appearance

Hobbits are much smaller than Men and generally smaller than the Khazâd. Their average height is around one metre, with variations between lineages. Their bodies are compact and sturdy rather than fragile.

Their feet are broad, tough and covered in thick hair. The soles are hard enough for them normally to go barefoot. Shoes are therefore uncommon and reserved for particular conditions.

Longevity and maturity

Hobbits live longer than ordinary Men. Many reach eighty or ninety years of age, and some live beyond one hundred. In the Shire, thirty-three is traditionally the age of majority.

They age slowly and may remain active for much of their lives. Elderly Hobbits often play an important role in family and local memory, especially regarding genealogies, property and old stories.

Health and endurance

Hobbits are generally healthy but possess no supernatural resistance to disease. Their rural way of life, regular diet and sturdy constitution give them good resistance to ordinary exertion.

They cope with long marches better than their size might suggest. Their endurance is based more on steady persistence than on speed or raw strength.

Senses and stealth

Hobbit senses are similar to those of Men and they possess no special night vision. They do, however, have good awareness of their immediate surroundings and readily notice changes in familiar places.

Their ability to move quietly is one of their most characteristic traits. Their small size, barefoot gait and habit of avoiding noisy surfaces allow them to approach without being heard. This racial ability should complement, not replace, skills in Concealment and Stealthy Movement.

Moral resistance

Hobbits are less attracted than many other peoples by power, domination and glory. They generally desire a safe home, a stable life, good harvests, food and the company of those close to them. This lack of ambition makes them relatively difficult to corrupt with promises of power.

They are not immune to the Shadow. Fear, jealousy, possessiveness or the desire to protect their own can still be exploited. Their resistance comes chiefly from the fact that the most common forms of temptation hold little appeal for them.

Temperament

Hobbits are generally cautious, sociable and attached to habit. They take great interest in the affairs of their family and neighbours, while often remaining wary of distant events, strangers and sudden change.

They value common sense and practical solutions. Grand speeches, titles and highly ambitious projects impress them little when they produce no practical result.

Family and society

Family lies at the centre of Hobbit society. Kinship is known in precise detail and extended families maintain regular relations through marriages, visits, inheritance and celebrations. The family name carries strong social importance.

Marriage is generally monogamous. Children grow up in a communal environment in which parents, uncles, aunts, cousins and neighbours all take part in their upbringing. Differences in wealth exist, but they do not produce a warrior nobility comparable to that of many human kingdoms.

Authority, customs and property

Hobbit institutions are simple and authorities generally possess limited powers. Local custom, reputation and social pressure settle much of everyday conflict. Questions of property, boundaries, inheritance and succession are nevertheless taken very seriously.

Objects passed down within a family often have great value because of their history. Gifts, birthdays and exchanges between families play a significant role in social life.

Homes and comfort

Hobbits are famous for dwellings dug into hills, often called Hobbit-holes or smials. The largest may contain many bedrooms, kitchens, sitting rooms, cellars, pantries and corridors. Other Hobbits live in houses built above ground where the terrain is better suited to them.

They place great value on comfort, cleanliness, warmth and stores of food. Their idea of prosperity rests more on a well-kept home and fertile land than on monuments or treasure.

Agriculture, gardening and food

Agriculture forms the basis of many Hobbit communities. They grow grains, vegetables, fruit, herbs, hops and various useful plants. Gardening is widespread, and some Hobbits possess excellent practical knowledge of local flora.

Food occupies an important place in daily life. They enjoy several meals, family recipes, communal dining and inns. Beer and, in later periods, pipe-weed are among the best-known traditions of the Shire.

Craft and trade

Hobbits are good craftsmen in fields useful to everyday life: carpentry, sewing, cooking, pottery, farming and the making of small tools. They seldom produce military equipment, heavy armour or large stone buildings.

Trade exists mainly on a regional scale. Communities may import metal, tools and cloth and export food, beer, agricultural produce and craftwork. Few Hobbits become long-distance merchants.

Weapons and war

Most Hobbits receive little advanced military training. Knives, staves, slings, short bows and farm tools are the most natural weapons. Weapons made for Men are often too large for them.

They are particularly skilful when throwing stones or using a sling. Their coordination and practice from childhood give them surprising accuracy. Armour is rare; when a community must defend itself, it relies on knowledge of the land, hedges, paths, missile fire and ambushes.

Magic and religion

Hobbits possess few organised magical traditions. Magic is generally associated with Elves, Wizards or ancient tales. A Hobbit can nevertheless learn magic if given appropriate training; magical professions should simply remain rare within traditional Cultures.

Their religion is little institutionalised. They have no great temples or visible clergy. Their spiritual life is chiefly tied to custom, family, the seasons, the land and the memory of the dead.

Relations with other peoples

Relations with Men are generally peaceful, even though the Big Folk often underestimate Hobbits. The Dúnedain of the North secretly protect the Shire during the Third Age, without most of its inhabitants understanding the importance of that protection.

For a long time Elves are almost legendary figures to Hobbits. Contact with the Khazâd is more practical through roads and trade. Orcs and other servants of the Shadow are dangerous enemies whom Hobbits prefer to avoid or fight at a distance.

The three great Cultures

Harfoots are the most numerous and are closely associated with hills, farmland and dug dwellings. Stoors are generally broader and more closely connected with rivers, fishing and wet country. Fallohides are often taller, fairer-haired and historically closer to Elves and woodland regions.

Les Hobbits sont beaucoup plus petits que les Hommes et généralement plus petits que les Khazâd. Leur taille moyenne se situe autour d’un mètre, avec des variations selon les lignées. Leur corps est compact et robuste plutôt que fragile.

Leurs pieds sont larges, solides et couverts d’un poil épais. La plante est suffisamment résistante pour qu’ils marchent habituellement pieds nus. Les chaussures sont donc rares et réservées à des conditions particulières.

Les Hobbits vivent plus longtemps que les Hommes ordinaires. Beaucoup atteignent quatre-vingts ou quatre-vingt-dix ans, et certains dépassent cent ans. Dans la Comté, trente-trois ans correspond traditionnellement à la majorité.

Ils vieillissent lentement et peuvent rester actifs pendant une grande partie de leur vie. Les Hobbits âgés jouent souvent un rôle important dans la mémoire familiale et locale, notamment pour les généalogies, les propriétés et les anciennes histoires.

Santé et endurance

Les Hobbits sont généralement en bonne santé mais ne possèdent pas de résistance surnaturelle aux maladies. Leur mode de vie rural, une alimentation régulière et leur constitution robuste leur donnent une bonne résistance aux efforts ordinaires.

Ils supportent mieux les longues marches qu’on pourrait l’imaginer au regard de leur taille. Leur endurance repose davantage sur la constance que sur la vitesse ou la force brute.

Sens et discrétion

Les sens des Hobbits sont proches de ceux des Hommes et ils ne possèdent pas de vision nocturne particulière. Ils ont cependant une bonne perception de leur environnement proche et remarquent facilement les changements dans un lieu familier.

Leur capacité à se déplacer silencieusement est l’un de leurs traits les plus caractéristiques. Leur petite taille, leur démarche pieds nus et leur habitude d’éviter les surfaces bruyantes leur permettent d’approcher sans être entendus. Cette aptitude raciale doit compléter, et non remplacer, les compétences de Dissimulation et de Déplacement furtif.

Résistance morale

Les Hobbits sont moins attirés que beaucoup d’autres peuples par le pouvoir, la domination et la gloire. Ils désirent généralement un foyer sûr, une vie stable, de bonnes récoltes, de la nourriture et la compagnie de leurs proches. Cette faible ambition les rend relativement difficiles à corrompre par les promesses de puissance.

Ils ne sont pas immunisés contre l’Ombre. La peur, la jalousie, la possession ou le désir de protéger les leurs peuvent toujours être exploités. Leur résistance vient surtout du fait que les formes les plus classiques de tentation ont peu d’intérêt pour eux.

Tempérament

Les Hobbits sont généralement prudents, sociables et attachés aux habitudes. Ils s’intéressent beaucoup aux affaires de leur famille et de leur voisinage, tout en se montrant souvent méfiants envers les événements lointains, les étrangers et les changements brusques.

Ils valorisent le bon sens et les solutions concrètes. Les grands discours, les titres et les projets très ambitieux les impressionnent peu lorsqu’ils ne produisent aucun résultat pratique.

Le mariage est généralement monogame. Les enfants grandissent dans un environnement communautaire où parents, oncles, tantes, cousins et voisins participent à leur éducation. Les différences de richesse existent, mais elles ne produisent pas une noblesse guerrière comparable à celle de nombreux royaumes humains.

Les institutions hobbits sont simples et les autorités disposent généralement de pouvoirs limités. Les coutumes locales, la réputation et la pression sociale règlent une grande partie des conflits. Hobbits — Kuduk

Hobbits, called Periannath in Sindarin and often Halflings by Men, are a small people related to Humans. They are sufficiently distinct in size, longevity, constitution and history to be treated as a Race of their own. For a long time they remain little known to the great peoples of Middle-earth, because their communities are small, rural and far removed from the principal wars.

Their earliest known homes lie east of the Misty Mountains, in the vale of the Anduin. During the Third Age, several groups migrated westward and gradually settled in Eriador. The three great Hobbit traditions are the Harfoots, Stoors and Fallohides. They should be treated as Cultures rather than as separate Races.

Migrations and settlement in Eriador

Hobbit migrations were gradual and extended over several generations. They were usually driven by the search for safe, fertile lands suited to their way of life rather than by conquest.

After several stages of settlement in Eriador, a large part of the Hobbit population established itself in the region that became the Shire. This land was granted to their ancestors by the authority of the Northern Kingdom. After the disappearance of Arnor's institutions, the Hobbits continued to live according to their own customs with very little outside interference.

Appearance

Hobbits are much smaller than Men and generally smaller than the Khazâd. Their average height is around one metre, with variations between lineages. Their bodies are compact and sturdy rather than fragile.

Their feet are broad, tough and covered in thick hair. The soles are hard enough for them normally to go barefoot. Shoes are therefore uncommon and reserved for particular conditions.

Longevity and maturity

Hobbits live longer than ordinary Men. Many reach eighty or ninety years of age, and some live beyond one hundred. In the Shire, thirty-three is traditionally the age of majority.

They age slowly and may remain active for much of their lives. Elderly Hobbits often play an important role in family and local memory, especially regarding genealogies, property and old stories.

Health and endurance

Hobbits are generally healthy but possess no supernatural resistance to disease. Their rural way of life, regular diet and sturdy constitution give them good resistance to ordinary exertion.

They cope with long marches better than their size might suggest. Their endurance is based more on steady persistence than on speed or raw strength.

Senses and stealth

Hobbit senses are similar to those of Men and they possess no special night vision. They do, however, have good awareness of their immediate surroundings and readily notice changes in familiar places.

Their ability to move quietly is one of their most characteristic traits. Their small size, barefoot gait and habit of avoiding noisy surfaces allow them to approach without being heard. This racial ability should complement, not replace, skills in Concealment and Stealthy Movement.

Moral resistance

Hobbits are less attracted than many other peoples by power, domination and glory. They generally desire a safe home, a stable life, good harvests, food and the company of those close to them. This lack of ambition makes them relatively difficult to corrupt with promises of power.

They are not immune to the Shadow. Fear, jealousy, possessiveness or the desire to protect their own can still be exploited. Their resistance comes chiefly from the fact that the most common forms of temptation hold little appeal for them.

Temperament

Hobbits are generally cautious, sociable and attached to habit. They take great interest in the affairs of their family and neighbours, while often remaining wary of distant events, strangers and sudden change.

They value common sense and practical solutions. Grand speeches, titles and highly ambitious projects impress them little when they produce no practical result.

Family and society

Family lies at the centre of Hobbit society. Kinship is known in precise detail and extended families maintain regular relations through marriages, visits, inheritance and celebrations. The family name carries strong social importance.

Marriage is generally monogamous. Children grow up in a communal environment in which parents, uncles, aunts, cousins and neighbours all take part in their upbringing. Differences in wealth exist, but they do not produce a warrior nobility comparable to that of many human kingdoms.

Authority, customs and property

Hobbit institutions are simple and authorities generally possess limited powers. Local custom, reputation and social pressure settle much of everyday conflict. Questions of property, boundaries, inheritance and succession are nevertheless taken very seriously.

Objects passed down within a family often have great value because of their history. Gifts, birthdays and exchanges between families play a significant role in social life.

Homes and comfort

Hobbits are famous for dwellings dug into hills, often called Hobbit-holes or smials. The largest may contain many bedrooms, kitchens, sitting rooms, cellars, pantries and corridors. Other Hobbits live in houses built above ground where the terrain is better suited to them.

They place great value on comfort, cleanliness, warmth and stores of food. Their idea of prosperity rests more on a well-kept home and fertile land than on monuments or treasure.

Agriculture, gardening and food

Agriculture forms the basis of many Hobbit communities. They grow grains, vegetables, fruit, herbs, hops and various useful plants. Gardening is widespread, and some Hobbits possess excellent practical knowledge of local flora.

Food occupies an important place in daily life. They enjoy several meals, family recipes, communal dining and inns. Beer and, in later periods, pipe-weed are among the best-known traditions of the Shire.

Craft and trade

Hobbits are good craftsmen in fields useful to everyday life: carpentry, sewing, cooking, pottery, farming and the making of small tools. They seldom produce military equipment, heavy armour or large stone buildings.

Trade exists mainly on a regional scale. Communities may import metal, tools and cloth and export food, beer, agricultural produce and craftwork. Few Hobbits become long-distance merchants.

Weapons and war

Most Hobbits receive little advanced military training. Knives, staves, slings, short bows and farm tools are the most natural weapons. Weapons made for Men are often too large for them.

They are particularly skilful when throwing stones or using a sling. Their coordination and practice from childhood give them surprising accuracy. Armour is rare; when a community must defend itself, it relies on knowledge of the land, hedges, paths, missile fire and ambushes.

Magic and religion

Hobbits possess few organised magical traditions. Magic is generally associated with Elves, Wizards or ancient tales. A Hobbit can nevertheless learn magic if given appropriate training; magical professions should simply remain rare within traditional Cultures.

Their religion is little institutionalised. They have no great temples or visible clergy. Their spiritual life is chiefly tied to custom, family, the seasons, the land and the memory of the dead.

Relations with other peoples

Hobbits — Kuduk

Hobbits, called Periannath in Sindarin and often Halflings by Men, are a small people related to Humans. They are sufficiently distinct in size, longevity, constitution and history to be treated as a Race of their own. For a long time they remain little known to the great peoples of Middle-earth, because their communities are small, rural and far removed from the principal wars.

Their earliest known homes lie east of the Misty Mountains, in the vale of the Anduin. During the Third Age, several groups migrated westward and gradually settled in Eriador. The three great Hobbit traditions are the Harfoots, Stoors and Fallohides. They should be treated as Cultures rather than as separate Races.

Migrations and settlement in Eriador

Hobbit migrations were gradual and extended over several generations. They were usually driven by the search for safe, fertile lands suited to their way of life rather than by conquest.

After several stages of settlement in Eriador, a large part of the Hobbit population established itself in the region that became the Shire. This land was granted to their ancestors by the authority of the Northern Kingdom. After the disappearance of Arnor's institutions, the Hobbits continued to live according to their own customs with very little outside interference.

Appearance

Hobbits are much smaller than Men and generally smaller than the Khazâd. Their average height is around one metre, with variations between lineages. Their bodies are compact and sturdy rather than fragile.

Their feet are broad, tough and covered in thick hair. The soles are hard enough for them normally to go barefoot. Shoes are therefore uncommon and reserved for particular conditions.

Longevity and maturity

Hobbits live longer than ordinary Men. Many reach eighty or ninety years of age, and some live beyond one hundred. In the Shire, thirty-three is traditionally the age of majority.

They age slowly and may remain active for much of their lives. Elderly Hobbits often play an important role in family and local memory, especially regarding genealogies, property and old stories.

Health and endurance

Hobbits are generally healthy but possess no supernatural resistance to disease. Their rural way of life, regular diet and sturdy constitution give them good resistance to ordinary exertion.

They cope with long marches better than their size might suggest. Their endurance is based more on steady persistence than on speed or raw strength.

Senses and stealth

Hobbit senses are similar to those of Men and they possess no special night vision. They do, however, have good awareness of their immediate surroundings and readily notice changes in familiar places.

Their ability to move quietly is one of their most characteristic traits. Their small size, barefoot gait and habit of avoiding noisy surfaces allow them to approach without being heard. This racial ability should complement, not replace, skills in Concealment and Stealthy Movement.

Moral resistance

Hobbits are less attracted than many other peoples by power, domination and glory. They generally desire a safe home, a stable life, good harvests, food and the company of those close to them. This lack of ambition makes them relatively difficult to corrupt with promises of power.

They are not immune to the Shadow. Fear, jealousy, possessiveness or the desire to protect their own can still be exploited. Their resistance comes chiefly from the fact that the most common forms of temptation hold little appeal for them.

Temperament

Hobbits are generally cautious, sociable and attached to habit. They take great interest in the affairs of their family and neighbours, while often remaining wary of distant events, strangers and sudden change.

They value common sense and practical solutions. Grand speeches, titles and highly ambitious projects impress them little when they produce no practical result.

Family and society

Family lies at the centre of Hobbit society. Kinship is known in precise detail and extended families maintain regular relations through marriages, visits, inheritance and celebrations. The family name carries strong social importance.

Marriage is generally monogamous. Children grow up in a communal environment in which parents, uncles, aunts, cousins and neighbours all take part in their upbringing. Differences in wealth exist, but they do not produce a warrior nobility comparable to that of many human kingdoms.

Authority, customs and property

Hobbit institutions are simple and authorities generally possess limited powers. Local custom, reputation and social pressure settle much of everyday conflict. Questions of property, boundaries, inheritance and succession are nevertheless taken very seriously.

Objects passed down within a family often have great value because of their history. Gifts, birthdays and exchanges between families play a significant role in social life.

Homes and comfort

Hobbits are famous for dwellings dug into hills, often called Hobbit-holes or smials. The largest may contain many bedrooms, kitchens, sitting rooms, cellars, pantries and corridors. Other Hobbits live in houses built above ground where the terrain is better suited to them.

They place great value on comfort, cleanliness, warmth and stores of food. Their idea of prosperity rests more on a well-kept home and fertile land than on monuments or treasure.

Agriculture, gardening and food

Agriculture forms the basis of many Hobbit communities. They grow grains, vegetables, fruit, herbs, hops and various useful plants. Gardening is widespread, and some Hobbits possess excellent practical knowledge of local flora.

Food occupies an important place in daily life. They enjoy several meals, family recipes, communal dining and inns. Beer and, in later periods, pipe-weed are among the best-known traditions of the Shire.

Craft and trade

Hobbits are good craftsmen in fields useful to everyday life: carpentry, sewing, cooking, pottery, farming and the making of small tools. They seldom produce military equipment, heavy armour or large stone buildings.

Trade exists mainly on a regional scale. Communities may import metal, tools and cloth and export food, beer, agricultural produce and craftwork. Few Hobbits become long-distance merchants.

Weapons and war

Most Hobbits receive little advanced military training. Knives, staves, slings, short bows and farm tools are the most natural weapons. Weapons made for Men are often too large for them.

Magic and religion

Hobbits possess few organised magical traditions. Magic is generally associated with Elves, Wizards or ancient tales. A Hobbit can nevertheless learn magic if given appropriate training; magical professions should simply remain rare within traditional Cultures.

Their religion is little institutionalised. They have no great temples or visible clergy. Their spiritual life is chiefly tied to custom, family, the seasons, the land and the memory of the dead.

Relations with other peoples

Relations with Men are generally peaceful, even though the Big Folk often underestimate Hobbits. The Dúnedain of the North secretly protect the Shire during the Third Age, without most of its inhabitants understanding the importance of that protection.

For a long time Elves are almost legendary figures to Hobbits. Contact with the Khazâd is more practical through roads and trade. Orcs and other servants of the Shadow are dangerous enemies whom Hobbits prefer to avoid or fight at a distance.

Harfoots are the most numerous and are closely associated with hills, farmland and dug dwellings. Stoors are generally broader and more closely connected with rivers, fishing and wet country. Fallohides are often taller, fairer-haired and historically closer to Elves and woodland regions.

These groups gradually mingled after their migration into Eriador. In later periods, a Hobbit may have ancestors from all three traditions; Culture then represents primarily the dominant upbringing and family heritage.

Professions and place in character creation

The Hobbits — Kuduk Race should represent the shared traits of Hobbit-kind: small stature, greater longevity than ordinary Men, tough feet, naturally quiet movement, good coordination and relative resistance to temptations based on ambition.

Leurs premiers foyers connus se trouvent à l’est des Monts Brumeux, dans la vallée de l’Anduin. Après plusieurs étapes en Eriador, une grande partie des Hobbits s’établit dans la région qui devint la Comté. Celle-ci fut accordée à leurs ancêtres par l’autorité du Royaume du Nord. Après la disparition des institutions d’Arnor, les Hobbits continuèrent à vivre selon leurs propres coutumes avec très peu d’intervention extérieure.

Apparence

Les Hobbits sont beaucoup plus petits que les Hommes et généralement plus petits que les Khazâd. Leur taille moyenne se situe autour d’un mètre, avec des variations selon les lignées. Leur corps est compact et robuste plutôt que fragile.

Leurs pieds sont larges, solides et couverts d’un poil épais. La plante est suffisamment résistante pour qu’ils marchent habituellement pieds nus. Les chaussures sont donc rares et réservées à des conditions particulières.

Longévité et maturité

Les Hobbits vivent plus longtemps que les Hommes ordinaires. Beaucoup atteignent quatre-vingts ou quatre-vingt-dix ans, et certains dépassent cent ans. Dans la Comté, trente-trois ans correspond traditionnellement à la majorité.

Ils vieillissent lentement et peuvent rester actifs pendant une grande partie de leur vie. Les Hobbits âgés jouent souvent un rôle important dans la mémoire familiale et locale, notamment pour les généalogies, les propriétés et les anciennes histoires.

Santé et endurance

Les Hobbits sont généralement en bonne santé mais ne possèdent pas de résistance surnaturelle aux maladies. Leur mode de vie rural, une alimentation régulière et leur constitution robuste leur donnent une bonne résistance aux efforts ordinaires.

Ils supportent mieux les longues marches qu’on pourrait l’imaginer au regard de leur taille. Leur endurance repose davantage sur la constance que sur la vitesse ou la force brute.

Sens et discrétion

Les sens des Hobbits sont proches de ceux des Hommes et ils ne possèdent pas de vision nocturne particulière. Ils ont cependant une bonne perception de leur environnement proche et remarquent facilement les changements dans un lieu familier.

Leur capacité à se déplacer silencieusement est l’un de leurs traits les plus caractéristiques. Leur petite taille, leur démarche pieds nus et leur habitude d’éviter les surfaces bruyantes leur permettent d’approcher sans être entendus. Cette aptitude raciale doit compléter, et non remplacer, les compétences de Dissimulation et de Déplacement furtif.

Résistance morale

Les Hobbits sont moins attirés que beaucoup d’autres peuples par le pouvoir, la domination et la gloire. Ils désirent généralement un foyer sûr, une vie stable, de bonnes récoltes, de la nourriture et la compagnie de leurs proches. Cette faible ambition les rend relativement difficiles à corrompre par les promesses de puissance.

Ils ne sont pas immunisés contre l’Ombre. La peur, la jalousie, la possession ou le désir de protéger les leurs peuvent toujours être exploités. Leur résistance vient surtout du fait que les formes les plus classiques de tentation ont peu d’intérêt pour eux.

Tempérament

Les Hobbits sont généralement prudents, sociables et attachés aux habitudes. Ils s’intéressent beaucoup aux affaires de leur famille et de leur voisinage, tout en se montrant souvent méfiants envers les événements lointains, les étrangers et les changements brusques.

Ils valorisent le bon sens et les solutions concrètes. Les grands discours, les titres et les projets très ambitieux les impressionnent peu lorsqu’ils ne produisent aucun résultat pratique.

Famille et société

La famille est au centre de la société hobbit. Les liens de parenté sont connus avec précision et les familles étendues entretiennent des relations régulières par les mariages, les visites, les héritages et les fêtes. Le nom de famille possède une forte importance sociale.

Le mariage est généralement monogame. Les enfants grandissent dans un environnement communautaire où parents, oncles, tantes, cousins et voisins participent à leur éducation. Les différences de richesse existent, mais elles ne produisent pas une noblesse guerrière comparable à celle de nombreux royaumes humains.

Autorité, coutumes et propriété

Les institutions hobbits sont simples et les autorités disposent généralement de pouvoirs limités. Les coutumes locales, la réputation et la pression sociale règlent une grande partie des conflits. Les questions de propriété, de limites de terrain, d’héritage et de succession sont néanmoins prises très au sérieux.

Les objets transmis dans une famille possèdent souvent une valeur importante en raison de leur histoire. Les cadeaux, les anniversaires et les échanges entre familles jouent un rôle notable dans la vie sociale.

Ils accordent une grande valeur au confort, à la propreté, à la chaleur et aux réserves de nourriture. Leur conception de la prospérité repose davantage sur un foyer bien entretenu et une terre fertile que sur les monuments ou les trésors.

Hobbits — Kuduk

Hobbits, called Periannath in Sindarin and often Halflings by Men, are a small people related to Humans. They are sufficiently distinct in size, longevity, constitution and history to be treated as a Race of their own. For a long time they remain little known to the great peoples of Middle-earth, because their communities are small, rural and far removed from the principal wars.

Their earliest known homes lie east of the Misty Mountains, in the vale of the Anduin. During the Third Age, several groups migrated westward and gradually settled in Eriador. The three great Hobbit traditions are the Harfoots, Stoors and Fallohides. They should be treated as Cultures rather than as separate Races.

Migrations and settlement in Eriador

Hobbit migrations were gradual and extended over several generations. They were usually driven by the search for safe, fertile lands suited to their way of life rather than by conquest.

After several stages of settlement in Eriador, a large part of the Hobbit population established itself in the region that became the Shire. This land was granted to their ancestors by the authority of the Northern Kingdom. After the disappearance of Arnor's institutions, the Hobbits continued to live according to their own customs with very little outside interference.

Appearance

Hobbits are much smaller than Men and generally smaller than the Khazâd. Their average height is around one metre, with variations between lineages. Their bodies are compact and sturdy rather than fragile.

Their feet are broad, tough and covered in thick hair. The soles are hard enough for them normally to go barefoot. Shoes are therefore uncommon and reserved for particular conditions.

Longevity and maturity

Hobbits live longer than ordinary Men. Many reach eighty or ninety years of age, and some live beyond one hundred. In the Shire, thirty-three is traditionally the age of majority.

They age slowly and may remain active for much of their lives. Elderly Hobbits often play an important role in family and local memory, especially regarding genealogies, property and old stories.

Health and endurance

Hobbits are generally healthy but possess no supernatural resistance to disease. Their rural way of life, regular diet and sturdy constitution give them good resistance to ordinary exertion.

They cope with long marches better than their size might suggest. Their endurance is based more on steady persistence than on speed or raw strength.

Senses and stealth

Hobbit senses are similar to those of Men and they possess no special night vision. They do, however, have good awareness of their immediate surroundings and readily notice changes in familiar places.

Their ability to move quietly is one of their most characteristic traits. Their small size, barefoot gait and habit of avoiding noisy surfaces allow them to approach without being heard. This racial ability should complement, not replace, skills in Concealment and Stealthy Movement.

Moral resistance

Hobbits are less attracted than many other peoples by power, domination and glory. They generally desire a safe home, a stable life, good harvests, food and the company of those close to them. This lack of ambition makes them relatively difficult to corrupt with promises of power.

They are not immune to the Shadow. Fear, jealousy, possessiveness or the desire to protect their own can still be exploited. Their resistance comes chiefly from the fact that the most common forms of temptation hold little appeal for them.

Temperament

Hobbits are generally cautious, sociable and attached to habit. They take great interest in the affairs of their family and neighbours, while often remaining wary of distant events, strangers and sudden change.

They value common sense and practical solutions. Grand speeches, titles and highly ambitious projects impress them little when they produce no practical result.

Family and society

Family lies at the centre of Hobbit society. Kinship is known in precise detail and extended families maintain regular relations through marriages, visits, inheritance and celebrations. The family name carries strong social importance.

Marriage is generally monogamous. Children grow up in a communal environment in which parents, uncles, aunts, cousins and neighbours all take part in their upbringing. Differences in wealth exist, but they do not produce a warrior nobility comparable to that of many human kingdoms.

Authority, customs and property

Hobbit institutions are simple and authorities generally possess limited powers. Local custom, reputation and social pressure settle much of everyday conflict. Questions of property, boundaries, inheritance and succession are nevertheless taken very seriously.

Objects passed down within a family often have great value because of their history. Gifts, birthdays and exchanges between families play a significant role in social life.

Homes and comfort

Hobbits are famous for dwellings dug into hills, often called Hobbit-holes or smials. The largest may contain many bedrooms, kitchens, sitting rooms, cellars, pantries and corridors. Other Hobbits live in houses built above ground where the terrain is better suited to them.

They place great value on comfort, cleanliness, warmth and stores of food. Their idea of prosperity rests more on a well-kept home and fertile land than on monuments or treasure.

Agriculture, gardening and food

Agriculture forms the basis of many Hobbit communities. They grow grains, vegetables, fruit, herbs, hops and various useful plants. Gardening is widespread, and some Hobbits possess excellent practical knowledge of local flora.

Food occupies an important place in daily life. They enjoy several meals, family recipes, communal dining and inns. Beer and, in later periods, pipe-weed are among the best-known traditions of the Shire.

Craft and trade

Hobbits are good craftsmen in fields useful to everyday life: carpentry, sewing, cooking, pottery, farming and the making of small tools. They seldom produce military equipment, heavy armour or large stone buildings.

Trade exists mainly on a regional scale. Communities may import metal, tools and cloth and export food, beer, agricultural produce and craftwork. Few Hobbits become long-distance merchants.

Most Hobbits receive little advanced military training. Knives, staves, slings, short bows and farm tools are the most natural weapons. Weapons made for Men are often too large for them.

For a long time Elves are almost legendary figures to Hobbits. Contact with the Khazâd is more practical through roads and trade. Orcs and other servants of the Shadow are dangerous enemies whom Hobbits prefer to avoid or fight at a distance.

Harfoots are the most numerous and are closely associated with hills, farmland and dug dwellings. Stoors are generally broader and more closely connected with rivers, fishing and wet country. Fallohides are often taller, fairer-haired and historically closer to Elves and woodland regions.

Professions and place in character creation

The Hobbits — Kuduk Race should represent the shared traits of Hobbit-kind: small stature, greater longevity than ordinary Men, tough feet, naturally quiet movement, good coordination and relative resistance to temptations based on ambition.

Leurs premiers foyers connus se trouvent à l’est des Monts Brumeux, dans la vallée de l’Anduin. Au cours du Troisième Âge, plusieurs groupes migrèrent vers l’ouest et s’établirent progressivement en Eriador. Les trois grandes traditions hobbits sont les Pieds-velus, les Forts et les Pâles. Les migrations hobbits furent progressives et s’étendirent sur plusieurs générations. Elles furent généralement motivées par la recherche de terres sûres, fertiles et adaptées à leur mode de vie plutôt que par la conquête.

Après plusieurs étapes en Eriador, une grande partie des Hobbits s’établit dans la région qui devint la Comté. Celle-ci fut accordée à leurs ancêtres par l’autorité du Royaume du Nord. Après la disparition des institutions d’Arnor, les Hobbits continuèrent à vivre selon leurs propres coutumes avec très peu d’intervention extérieure.

Apparence

Les Hobbits sont beaucoup plus petits que les Hommes et généralement plus petits que les Khazâd. Leur taille moyenne se situe autour d’un mètre, avec des variations selon les lignées. Leur corps est compact et robuste plutôt que fragile.

Leurs pieds sont larges, solides et couverts d’un poil épais. La plante est suffisamment résistante pour qu’ils marchent habituellement pieds nus. Les chaussures sont donc rares et réservées à des conditions particulières.

Longévité et maturité

Les Hobbits vivent plus longtemps que les Hommes ordinaires. Beaucoup atteignent quatre-vingts ou quatre-vingt-dix ans, et certains dépassent cent ans. Dans la Comté, trente-trois ans correspond traditionnellement à la majorité.

Ils vieillissent lentement et peuvent rester actifs pendant une grande partie de leur vie. Les Hobbits âgés jouent souvent un rôle important dans la mémoire familiale et locale, notamment pour les généalogies, les propriétés et les anciennes histoires.

Santé et endurance

Les Hobbits sont généralement en bonne santé mais ne possèdent pas de résistance surnaturelle aux maladies. Leur mode de vie rural, une alimentation régulière et leur constitution robuste leur donnent une bonne résistance aux efforts ordinaires.

Ils supportent mieux les longues marches qu’on pourrait l’imaginer au regard de leur taille. Leur endurance repose davantage sur la constance que sur la vitesse ou la force brute.

Sens et discrétion

Les sens des Hobbits sont proches de ceux des Hommes et ils ne possèdent pas de vision nocturne particulière. Ils ont cependant une bonne perception de leur environnement proche et remarquent facilement les changements dans un lieu familier.

Leur capacité à se déplacer silencieusement est l’un de leurs traits les plus caractéristiques. Leur petite taille, leur démarche pieds nus et leur habitude d’éviter les surfaces bruyantes leur permettent d’approcher sans être entendus. Résistance morale

Les Hobbits sont moins attirés que beaucoup d’autres peuples par le pouvoir, la domination et la gloire. Ils désirent généralement un foyer sûr, une vie stable, de bonnes récoltes, de la nourriture et la compagnie de leurs proches. Cette faible ambition les rend relativement difficiles à corrompre par les promesses de puissance.

Ils ne sont pas immunisés contre l’Ombre. La peur, la jalousie, la possession ou le désir de protéger les leurs peuvent toujours être exploités. Leur résistance vient surtout du fait que les formes les plus classiques de tentation ont peu d’intérêt pour eux.

Tempérament

Les Hobbits sont généralement prudents, sociables et attachés aux habitudes. Ils s’intéressent beaucoup aux affaires de leur famille et de leur voisinage, tout en se montrant souvent méfiants envers les événements lointains, les étrangers et les changements brusques.

Le mariage est généralement monogame. Les enfants grandissent dans un environnement communautaire où parents, oncles, tantes, cousins et voisins participent à leur éducation. Les institutions hobbits sont simples et les autorités disposent généralement de pouvoirs limités. Les coutumes locales, la réputation et la pression sociale règlent une grande partie des conflits. Hobbits — Kuduk

Hobbits, called Periannath in Sindarin and often Halflings by Men, are a small people related to Humans. They are sufficiently distinct in size, longevity, constitution and history to be treated as a Race of their own. For a long time they remain little known to the great peoples of Middle-earth, because their communities are small, rural and far removed from the principal wars.

Their earliest known homes lie east of the Misty Mountains, in the vale of the Anduin. During the Third Age, several groups migrated westward and gradually settled in Eriador. The three great Hobbit traditions are the Harfoots, Stoors and Fallohides. They should be treated as Cultures rather than as separate Races.

Migrations and settlement in Eriador

Hobbit migrations were gradual and extended over several generations. They were usually driven by the search for safe, fertile lands suited to their way of life rather than by conquest.

After several stages of settlement in Eriador, a large part of the Hobbit population established itself in the region that became the Shire. This land was granted to their ancestors by the authority of the Northern Kingdom. After the disappearance of Arnor's institutions, the Hobbits continued to live according to their own customs with very little outside interference.

Appearance

Hobbits are much smaller than Men and generally smaller than the Khazâd. Their average height is around one metre, with variations between lineages. Their bodies are compact and sturdy rather than fragile.

Their feet are broad, tough and covered in thick hair. The soles are hard enough for them normally to go barefoot. Shoes are therefore uncommon and reserved for particular conditions.

Longevity and maturity

Hobbits live longer than ordinary Men. Many reach eighty or ninety years of age, and some live beyond one hundred. In the Shire, thirty-three is traditionally the age of majority.

They age slowly and may remain active for much of their lives. Elderly Hobbits often play an important role in family and local memory, especially regarding genealogies, property and old stories.

Health and endurance

Hobbits are generally healthy but possess no supernatural resistance to disease. Their rural way of life, regular diet and sturdy constitution give them good resistance to ordinary exertion.

They cope with long marches better than their size might suggest. Their endurance is based more on steady persistence than on speed or raw strength.

Senses and stealth

Hobbit senses are similar to those of Men and they possess no special night vision. They do, however, have good awareness of their immediate surroundings and readily notice changes in familiar places.

Their ability to move quietly is one of their most characteristic traits. Their small size, barefoot gait and habit of avoiding noisy surfaces allow them to approach without being heard. This racial ability should complement, not replace, skills in Concealment and Stealthy Movement.

Moral resistance

Hobbits are less attracted than many other peoples by power, domination and glory. They generally desire a safe home, a stable life, good harvests, food and the company of those close to them. This lack of ambition makes them relatively difficult to corrupt with promises of power.

They are not immune to the Shadow. Fear, jealousy, possessiveness or the desire to protect their own can still be exploited. Their resistance comes chiefly from the fact that the most common forms of temptation hold little appeal for them.

Temperament

Hobbits are generally cautious, sociable and attached to habit. They take great interest in the affairs of their family and neighbours, while often remaining wary of distant events, strangers and sudden change.

They value common sense and practical solutions. Grand speeches, titles and highly ambitious projects impress them little when they produce no practical result.

Family and society

Family lies at the centre of Hobbit society. Kinship is known in precise detail and extended families maintain regular relations through marriages, visits, inheritance and celebrations. The family name carries strong social importance.

Marriage is generally monogamous. Children grow up in a communal environment in which parents, uncles, aunts, cousins and neighbours all take part in their upbringing. Differences in wealth exist, but they do not produce a warrior nobility comparable to that of many human kingdoms.

Authority, customs and property

Hobbit institutions are simple and authorities generally possess limited powers. Local custom, reputation and social pressure settle much of everyday conflict. Questions of property, boundaries, inheritance and succession are nevertheless taken very seriously.

Objects passed down within a family often have great value because of their history. Gifts, birthdays and exchanges between families play a significant role in social life.

Homes and comfort

Hobbits are famous for dwellings dug into hills, often called Hobbit-holes or smials. The largest may contain many bedrooms, kitchens, sitting rooms, cellars, pantries and corridors. Other Hobbits live in houses built above ground where the terrain is better suited to them.

Agriculture forms the basis of many Hobbit communities. They grow grains, vegetables, fruit, herbs, hops and various useful plants. Gardening is widespread, and some Hobbits possess excellent practical knowledge of local flora.

Hobbits are good craftsmen in fields useful to everyday life: carpentry, sewing, cooking, pottery, farming and the making of small tools. They seldom produce military equipment, heavy armour or large stone buildings.

Trade exists mainly on a regional scale. Communities may import metal, tools and cloth and export food, beer, agricultural produce and craftwork. Few Hobbits become long-distance merchants.

Most Hobbits receive little advanced military training. Knives, staves, slings, short bows and farm tools are the most natural weapons. Weapons made for Men are often too large for them.

They are particularly skilful when throwing stones or using a sling. Their coordination and practice from childhood give them surprising accuracy. Armour is rare; when a community must defend itself, it relies on knowledge of the land, hedges, paths, missile fire and ambushes.

Hobbits possess few organised magical traditions. Magic is generally associated with Elves, Wizards or ancient tales. A Hobbit can nevertheless learn magic if given appropriate training; magical professions should simply remain rare within traditional Cultures.

Their religion is little institutionalised. They have no great temples or visible clergy. Their spiritual life is chiefly tied to custom, family, the seasons, the land and the memory of the dead.

Harfoots are the most numerous and are closely associated with hills, farmland and dug dwellings. Stoors are generally broader and more closely connected with rivers, fishing and wet country. Fallohides are often taller, fairer-haired and historically closer to Elves and woodland regions.

Professions and place in character creation

The Hobbits — Kuduk Race should represent the shared traits of Hobbit-kind: small stature, greater longevity than ordinary Men, tough feet, naturally quiet movement, good coordination and relative resistance to temptations based on ambition.

Leurs premiers foyers connus se trouvent à l’est des Monts Brumeux, dans la vallée de l’Anduin. Au cours du Troisième Âge, plusieurs groupes migrèrent vers l’ouest et s’établirent progressivement en Eriador. Les trois grandes traditions hobbits sont les Pieds-velus, les Forts et les Pâles. Les migrations hobbits furent progressives et s’étendirent sur plusieurs générations. Elles furent généralement motivées par la recherche de terres sûres, fertiles et adaptées à leur mode de vie plutôt que par la conquête.

Après plusieurs étapes en Eriador, une grande partie des Hobbits s’établit dans la région qui devint la Comté. Celle-ci fut accordée à leurs ancêtres par l’autorité du Royaume du Nord. Après la disparition des institutions d’Arnor, les Hobbits continuèrent à vivre selon leurs propres coutumes avec très peu d’intervention extérieure.

Apparence

Les Hobbits sont beaucoup plus petits que les Hommes et généralement plus petits que les Khazâd. Leur taille moyenne se situe autour d’un mètre, avec des variations selon les lignées. Leur corps est compact et robuste plutôt que fragile.

Leurs pieds sont larges, solides et couverts d’un poil épais. La plante est suffisamment résistante pour qu’ils marchent habituellement pieds nus. Les chaussures sont donc rares et réservées à des conditions particulières.

Longévité et maturité

Les Hobbits vivent plus longtemps que les Hommes ordinaires. Beaucoup atteignent quatre-vingts ou quatre-vingt-dix ans, et certains dépassent cent ans. Dans la Comté, trente-trois ans correspond traditionnellement à la majorité.

Ils vieillissent lentement et peuvent rester actifs pendant une grande partie de leur vie. Les Hobbits âgés jouent souvent un rôle important dans la mémoire familiale et locale, notamment pour les généalogies, les propriétés et les anciennes histoires.

Santé et endurance

Les Hobbits sont généralement en bonne santé mais ne possèdent pas de résistance surnaturelle aux maladies. Leur mode de vie rural, une alimentation régulière et leur constitution robuste leur donnent une bonne résistance aux efforts ordinaires.

Ils supportent mieux les longues marches qu’on pourrait l’imaginer au regard de leur taille. Leur endurance repose davantage sur la constance que sur la vitesse ou la force brute.

Sens et discrétion

Les sens des Hobbits sont proches de ceux des Hommes et ils ne possèdent pas de vision nocturne particulière. Ils ont cependant une bonne perception de leur environnement proche et remarquent facilement les changements dans un lieu familier.

Leur capacité à se déplacer silencieusement est l’un de leurs traits les plus caractéristiques. Résistance morale

Les Hobbits sont moins attirés que beaucoup d’autres peuples par le pouvoir, la domination et la gloire. Ils désirent généralement un foyer sûr, une vie stable, de bonnes récoltes, de la nourriture et la compagnie de leurs proches. Cette faible ambition les rend relativement difficiles à corrompre par les promesses de puissance.

Ils ne sont pas immunisés contre l’Ombre. La peur, la jalousie, la possession ou le désir de protéger les leurs peuvent toujours être exploités. Leur résistance vient surtout du fait que les formes les plus classiques de tentation ont peu d’intérêt pour eux.

Hobbits — Kuduk

Hobbits, called Periannath in Sindarin and often Halflings by Men, are a small people related to Humans. They are sufficiently distinct in size, longevity, constitution and history to be treated as a Race of their own. For a long time they remain little known to the great peoples of Middle-earth, because their communities are small, rural and far removed from the principal wars.

Their earliest known homes lie east of the Misty Mountains, in the vale of the Anduin. During the Third Age, several groups migrated westward and gradually settled in Eriador. The three great Hobbit traditions are the Harfoots, Stoors and Fallohides. They should be treated as Cultures rather than as separate Races.

Migrations and settlement in Eriador

Hobbit migrations were gradual and extended over several generations. They were usually driven by the search for safe, fertile lands suited to their way of life rather than by conquest.

After several stages of settlement in Eriador, a large part of the Hobbit population established itself in the region that became the Shire. This land was granted to their ancestors by the authority of the Northern Kingdom. After the disappearance of Arnor's institutions, the Hobbits continued to live according to their own customs with very little outside interference.

Appearance

Hobbits are much smaller than Men and generally smaller than the Khazâd. Their average height is around one metre, with variations between lineages. Their bodies are compact and sturdy rather than fragile.

Their feet are broad, tough and covered in thick hair. The soles are hard enough for them normally to go barefoot. Shoes are therefore uncommon and reserved for particular conditions.

Longevity and maturity

Hobbits live longer than ordinary Men. Many reach eighty or ninety years of age, and some live beyond one hundred. In the Shire, thirty-three is traditionally the age of majority.

They age slowly and may remain active for much of their lives. Elderly Hobbits often play an important role in family and local memory, especially regarding genealogies, property and old stories.

Health and endurance

Hobbits are generally healthy but possess no supernatural resistance to disease. Their rural way of life, regular diet and sturdy constitution give them good resistance to ordinary exertion.

They cope with long marches better than their size might suggest. Their endurance is based more on steady persistence than on speed or raw strength.

Senses and stealth

Hobbit senses are similar to those of Men and they possess no special night vision. They do, however, have good awareness of their immediate surroundings and readily notice changes in familiar places.

Their ability to move quietly is one of their most characteristic traits. Their small size, barefoot gait and habit of avoiding noisy surfaces allow them to approach without being heard. This racial ability should complement, not replace, skills in Concealment and Stealthy Movement.

Moral resistance

Hobbits are less attracted than many other peoples by power, domination and glory. They generally desire a safe home, a stable life, good harvests, food and the company of those close to them. This lack of ambition makes them relatively difficult to corrupt with promises of power.

They are not immune to the Shadow. Fear, jealousy, possessiveness or the desire to protect their own can still be exploited. Their resistance comes chiefly from the fact that the most common forms of temptation hold little appeal for them.

Temperament

Hobbits are generally cautious, sociable and attached to habit. They take great interest in the affairs of their family and neighbours, while often remaining wary of distant events, strangers and sudden change.

They value common sense and practical solutions. Grand speeches, titles and highly ambitious projects impress them little when they produce no practical result.

Family and society

Family lies at the centre of Hobbit society. Kinship is known in precise detail and extended families maintain regular relations through marriages, visits, inheritance and celebrations. The family name carries strong social importance.

Marriage is generally monogamous. Children grow up in a communal environment in which parents, uncles, aunts, cousins and neighbours all take part in their upbringing. Differences in wealth exist, but they do not produce a warrior nobility comparable to that of many human kingdoms.

Authority, customs and property

Hobbit institutions are simple and authorities generally possess limited powers. Local custom, reputation and social pressure settle much of everyday conflict. Questions of property, boundaries, inheritance and succession are nevertheless taken very seriously.

Objects passed down within a family often have great value because of their history. Gifts, birthdays and exchanges between families play a significant role in social life.

Homes and comfort

Hobbits are famous for dwellings dug into hills, often called Hobbit-holes or smials. The largest may contain many bedrooms, kitchens, sitting rooms, cellars, pantries and corridors. Other Hobbits live in houses built above ground where the terrain is better suited to them.

They place great value on comfort, cleanliness, warmth and stores of food. Their idea of prosperity rests more on a well-kept home and fertile land than on monuments or treasure.

Agriculture, gardening and food

Agriculture forms the basis of many Hobbit communities. They grow grains, vegetables, fruit, herbs, hops and various useful plants. Gardening is widespread, and some Hobbits possess excellent practical knowledge of local flora.

Food occupies an important place in daily life. They enjoy several meals, family recipes, communal dining and inns. Beer and, in later periods, pipe-weed are among the best-known traditions of the Shire.

Craft and trade

Hobbits are good craftsmen in fields useful to everyday life: carpentry, sewing, cooking, pottery, farming and the making of small tools. They seldom produce military equipment, heavy armour or large stone buildings.

Trade exists mainly on a regional scale. Communities may import metal, tools and cloth and export food, beer, agricultural produce and craftwork. Few Hobbits become long-distance merchants.

Weapons and war

Most Hobbits receive little advanced military training. Knives, staves, slings, short bows and farm tools are the most natural weapons. Weapons made for Men are often too large for them.

They are particularly skilful when throwing stones or using a sling. Their coordination and practice from childhood give them surprising accuracy. Armour is rare; when a community must defend itself, it relies on knowledge of the land, hedges, paths, missile fire and ambushes.

Magic and religion

Hobbits possess few organised magical traditions. Magic is generally associated with Elves, Wizards or ancient tales. A Hobbit can nevertheless learn magic if given appropriate training; magical professions should simply remain rare within traditional Cultures.

Their religion is little institutionalised. They have no great temples or visible clergy. Their spiritual life is chiefly tied to custom, family, the seasons, the land and the memory of the dead.

Relations with other peoples

Relations with Men are generally peaceful, even though the Big Folk often underestimate Hobbits. The Dúnedain of the North secretly protect the Shire during the Third Age, without most of its inhabitants understanding the importance of that protection.

For a long time Elves are almost legendary figures to Hobbits. Contact with the Khazâd is more practical through roads and trade. Orcs and other servants of the Shadow are dangerous enemies whom Hobbits prefer to avoid or fight at a distance.

Harfoots are the most numerous and are closely associated with hills, farmland and dug dwellings. Stoors are generally broader and more closely connected with rivers, fishing and wet country. Fallohides are often taller, fairer-haired and historically closer to Elves and woodland regions.

These groups gradually mingled after their migration into Eriador. In later periods, a Hobbit may have ancestors from all three traditions; Culture then represents primarily the dominant upbringing and family heritage.

Professions and place in character creation

The Hobbits — Kuduk Race should represent the shared traits of Hobbit-kind: small stature, greater longevity than ordinary Men, tough feet, naturally quiet movement, good coordination and relative resistance to temptations based on ambition.

Professional restrictions should be defined mainly by Culture. Fighters exist but remain uncommon, and users of magic are rare. After choosing the Race, the player selects Harfoot, Stoor or Fallohide Culture according to the era and origin of the character.

Ils restent longtemps peu connus des grands peuples de la Terre du Milieu, car leurs communautés sont petites, rurales et éloignées des principales guerres.

Leurs premiers foyers connus se trouvent à l’est des Monts Brumeux, dans la vallée de l’Anduin. Au cours du Troisième Âge, plusieurs groupes migrèrent vers l’ouest et s’établirent progressivement en Eriador. Les trois grandes traditions hobbits sont les Pieds-velus, les Forts et les Pâles. Migrations et installation en Eriador

Les migrations hobbits furent progressives et s’étendirent sur plusieurs générations. Elles furent généralement motivées par la recherche de terres sûres, fertiles et adaptées à leur mode de vie plutôt que par la conquête.

Après plusieurs étapes en Eriador, une grande partie des Hobbits s’établit dans la région qui devint la Comté. Celle-ci fut accordée à leurs ancêtres par l’autorité du Royaume du Nord. Après la disparition des institutions d’Arnor, les Hobbits continuèrent à vivre selon leurs propres coutumes avec très peu d’intervention extérieure.

Apparence

Les Hobbits sont beaucoup plus petits que les Hommes et généralement plus petits que les Khazâd. Leur taille moyenne se situe autour d’un mètre, avec des variations selon les lignées. Leur corps est compact et robuste plutôt que fragile.

Leurs pieds sont larges, solides et couverts d’un poil épais. La plante est suffisamment résistante pour qu’ils marchent habituellement pieds nus. Les chaussures sont donc rares et réservées à des conditions particulières.

Longévité et maturité

Les Hobbits vivent plus longtemps que les Hommes ordinaires. Beaucoup atteignent quatre-vingts ou quatre-vingt-dix ans, et certains dépassent cent ans. Dans la Comté, trente-trois ans correspond traditionnellement à la majorité.

Ils vieillissent lentement et peuvent rester actifs pendant une grande partie de leur vie. Les Hobbits âgés jouent souvent un rôle important dans la mémoire familiale et locale, notamment pour les généalogies, les propriétés et les anciennes histoires.

Santé et endurance

Les Hobbits sont généralement en bonne santé mais ne possèdent pas de résistance surnaturelle aux maladies. Leur mode de vie rural, une alimentation régulière et leur constitution robuste leur donnent une bonne résistance aux efforts ordinaires.

Ils supportent mieux les longues marches qu’on pourrait l’imaginer au regard de leur taille. Leur endurance repose davantage sur la constance que sur la vitesse ou la force brute.

Sens et discrétion

Les sens des Hobbits sont proches de ceux des Hommes et ils ne possèdent pas de vision nocturne particulière. Ils ont cependant une bonne perception de leur environnement proche et remarquent facilement les changements dans un lieu familier.

Leur capacité à se déplacer silencieusement est l’un de leurs traits les plus caractéristiques. Leur petite taille, leur démarche pieds nus et leur habitude d’éviter les surfaces bruyantes leur permettent d’approcher sans être entendus. Résistance morale

Les Hobbits sont moins attirés que beaucoup d’autres peuples par le pouvoir, la domination et la gloire. Ils désirent généralement un foyer sûr, une vie stable, de bonnes récoltes, de la nourriture et la compagnie de leurs proches. Cette faible ambition les rend relativement difficiles à corrompre par les promesses de puissance.
